In the past couple weeks, as Claude Code Skills emerged, I stopped primarily using rulesync because the latest features can't be represented in rulesync's format yet.
1 - assume users will store AI code configs some AI coding tool's native format, whether that's cursor, claude code, or any of the many tools that are out there

Rulesync can fetch skills from external repositories using the rulesync/install command. Instead of manually running fetch for each skill source, declare them in your rulesync.jsonc and run rulesync install to resolve and fetch them. Then rulesync/generate picks them up as local curated skills. Typical workflow: rulesync install && rulesync generate.
This lets you import sources from another repository
Add a sources array to your rulesync.jsonc:
The skills/ directory (or the path specified in the source URL) is listed from the remote repository.
To add one source without editing rulesync.jsonc by hand, run rulesync add <source>. It preserves existing comments, appends the source entry, installs it, and updates the appropriate lockfile.
The same source/add syntax works against a private GitHub repo's skills/ or rulesync/skills directory — the GitHub transport just needs credentials.
It uses the GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN environment variable:
Or pass a token explicitly: rulesync install --token ghp_xxxx.
Git transport (transport: "git", e.g. SSH remotes) relies on local git credential configuration instead.
Using local git auth (e.g. Git Credential Manager) instead of GITHUB_TOKEN
The plain owner/repo shorthand always uses the default "github" transport, which reads only GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN — it never consults local git credentials.

This Agent/Skills skill is the "linux kernel" of how I use AI with Logseq. The basic idea is that it points agents to look at the Logseq/Entity namespace for how to create and maintain the types of things I want to put in the garden.
This skill is inherited by all my Logseq knowledge gardens, and it's even got a descendent in Obsidian that I use.

My goal is to keep this skill tight and free from domain-specific info, so that pages in the garden are the sole source of information about how gardening is done in the garden. This is still a work in progress, though. If I do my job right, this skill will get smaller and smaller over time, and the variety of things I track in Logseq/Entity namespace will increase.

The reason this is important is that different gardens track different things, and also I use different AI Agent Harnesses. This one skill's job is to ensure all my Logseq gardens organize their information according to certain documented principles without having to redo AI skills again and again, particularly since Skills are not displayed in the garden, and information that's garden-specific should be stored in the garden.
